passages.happening:
Moses begins with the great command again. “You shall therefore love the LORD your God and always keep His charge, His statutes, His ordinances, and His commandments” (verse 1).

Then he makes a point about who he is talking to. It is not their children who have known God's discipline, his greatness, ‘His mighty hand, and His outstretched arm’ (verse 2). The children did not see what God did in Egypt to Pharaoh, or how the waters of the Red Sea closed over the Egyptian army (verses 3-4). They did not see what he did in the wilderness (verse 5), or what happened to Dathan and Abiram, when ‘the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them’ (verse 6).

“For it is your own eyes that have seen every great work that the LORD has done” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Many of the people Moses is speaking to were young at the exodus. They are among the last alive who saw the sea open.

Moses presses that on them. They are eyewitnesses. Their children are not. If what they saw is going to reach the next generation, it will have to be told.

He names two kinds of events. The first is God's acts against Egypt, the enemy outside. The second is God's judgment on Dathan and Abiram, who were Israelites. They rose against Moses, and the story is told in Numbers 16. The God who rescued Israel from Pharaoh also judged rebellion inside the camp. The people have seen both, and Moses will not let them remember only the first.

The word ‘discipline’ in verse 2 takes up the picture of chapter 8, a father training his son. All of it, the rescue and the judgments, was God bringing up his people.

Verse 1 says ‘therefore’. It points back to the end of chapter 10, to the seventy who became as many as the stars. Love is the answer to what God has done.
passages.later:
Numbers tells what happened to the rebels: ‘the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them and their households’ (Numbers 16:32).

A psalm takes up the duty that Moses lays on the eyewitnesses: “We will not hide them from their children, but will declare to the next generation the praises of the LORD and His might” (Psalm 78:4).

The book of Judges records what happened when the telling stopped: “another generation rose up who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel” (Judges 2:10).
passages.asks: Moses tells the eyewitnesses that their children did not see what they saw. Ask what you have seen God do that the younger people around you know nothing about, because no one has told them. And ask whether you remember only the comforting half of your story with God, or the correcting half as well.

passages.t: A land that drinks rain from heaven
passages.happening:
Moses calls them to keep every command, so that they will have strength to take the land and live long in it (verses 8-9).

Then he describes the land by comparing it with Egypt. “For the land that you are entering to possess is not like the land of Egypt, from which you have come, where you sowed your seed and irrigated on foot, like a vegetable garden” (verse 10). The new land ‘is a land of mountains and valleys that drinks in the rain from heaven’ (verse 11). “It is a land for which the LORD your God cares; the eyes of the LORD your God are always on it, from the beginning to the end of the year” (verse 12).

If Israel loves and serves God, he ‘will provide rain for your land in season, the autumn and spring rains’ (verse 14), with grain, new wine and oil, and grass for the herds. But if they turn to other gods, “He will shut the heavens so that there will be no rain” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The comparison would have been vivid to people whose parents farmed in Egypt. Egypt had the Nile. Its fields were watered by the river's yearly flood and by channels that farmers opened and closed by hand and foot. A farmer there could look at the river and know where his water was coming from.

Canaan had no great river. Its farms lived on rain, and the rain came in two seasons. The autumn rains softened the ground for plowing and sowing. The spring rains brought the grain to harvest. If either failed, people went hungry.

So the land itself would teach Israel to depend on God. In Egypt a man could water his own garden. In Canaan he could only look up. Moses presents this as a good thing: it is a land that God looks after himself, all year long.

It also explains the great temptation Israel would face. The Canaanites worshiped Baal as the god of the storm, the one who brought the rain. When rain is life and death, a rain god is hard to resist. Moses insists that the rain comes from the LORD. Verse 16 warns that the heart can be ‘enticed’. No one sets out to leave God. A person is drawn off toward whatever seems to promise the harvest.

The promise and the warning of verses 13 to 17 are spoken to Israel as a people, about its life in this land. The hard question below takes up how they should be read.
passages.later:
The prophet Elijah announced the warning of verse 17 to a king who had given Israel over to Baal: ‘there will be neither dew nor rain in these years except at my word’ (1 Kings 17:1).

Jeremiah put Moses' point as a question: “Can the worthless idols of the nations bring rain?” (Jeremiah 14:22).

Jesus said that the Father ‘sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous’ (Matthew 5:45). And Paul told a crowd who had never heard of Moses that the rain was God's witness to them: “He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness” (Acts 14:17).
passages.hard:
Do these verses promise that faithful people will always do well, and that hardship is always punishment?

Verses 13 to 17 link Israel's obedience to rain and harvest, and its idol worship to drought. Some have read passages like this as a promise that faith brings wealth and health to each believer. That is the claim at the center of what is called prosperity teaching.

Most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, reject that reading. The promises are made to the nation of Israel, inside a particular covenant tied to a particular land. They describe the shape of that covenant over time. They are not a formula for each person's circumstances.

The rest of the Old Testament pushes back against a mechanical reading. Job suffers though he is righteous. Several psalms and the book of Ecclesiastes complain that the wicked often do well. Jesus rejected the idea that suffering proves sin. Of eighteen people killed by a falling tower he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem?” and answered, “No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5).

The chapter should not be emptied of meaning either. It teaches that the world belongs to God, that faithfulness and unfaithfulness matter, and that a people's life with God affects their life together.

So a drought, an illness or a loss is not to be read as God's verdict on the person who suffers it, and no one should be told that it is.
passages.asks: In Egypt a farmer could water his own field. In Canaan he had to look up. Ask which kind of life you would choose, and why. Then ask where in your life you cannot make the rain come, and whether you treat that as a threat or as the place where you are learning to trust.

passages.t: Fix these words in your hearts
passages.happening:
Moses repeats what he said after the Shema. “Fix these words of mine in your hearts and minds; tie them as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. Teach them to your children, speaking about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. Write them on the doorposts of your houses and on your gates” (verses 18-20).

He adds the aim: that their days and their children's days in the land may be many, ‘as long as the heavens are above the earth’ (verse 21).

If they hold fast to God, he will drive out the nations before them. “Every place where the sole of your foot treads will be yours” (verse 24). The land will reach from the wilderness to Lebanon, and from the Euphrates River to the Western Sea.
passages.hearers:
These verses are almost word for word the same as 6:6-9. The repetition is deliberate. The whole sermon of chapters 6 to 11 is held between the two, like a picture in a frame. Moses began this part of the book with the words on the heart, the children, the hand, the forehead and the door, and he ends it there.

Jewish tradition joined these verses with 6:4-9 and with a passage from Numbers 15 as the three paragraphs of the Shema, recited each evening and each morning. The small case fixed to the doorframe of a Jewish home, the mezuzah, holds both passages from Deuteronomy.

The order in verse 18 is the same as in chapter 6. The words go into the heart first. Only then do they go out to the children, the body and the house. A parent cannot hand on what he does not have.

The borders in verse 24 describe the widest reach of the promise. Israel came nearest to them under King David and King Solomon. The verse is a promise made to Israel at the Jordan in the time of Moses. These notes draw nothing from it about any border or any conflict today.

The driving out of the nations in verse 23 belongs with the command of chapter 7. The note on chapter 7, verses 1 to 5, sets out how Christians read it.
passages.later:
God repeated the promise to Joshua after Moses died: “I have given you every place where the sole of your foot will tread, just as I promised to Moses” (Joshua 1:3).

The book of Kings says of Solomon's time, “And Solomon reigned over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines, as far as the border of Egypt” (1 Kings 4:21).

The book of Proverbs asks a child to keep a parent's teaching in the way Moses describes: “bind them around your neck, write them on the tablet of your heart” (Proverbs 3:3).
passages.asks: Moses says the same thing at the end of his sermon that he said at the start. Ask what you need to hear again and again because you do not keep hold of it. And look at the order: heart first, then children. Ask whether the faith you hope to pass on is alive in you.

passages.t: A blessing and a curse, and two mountains
passages.happening:
Moses brings the sermon to its point. He is setting before Israel ‘a blessing and a curse’ (verse 26). The blessing will come ‘if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God’ (verse 27). The curse will come if they turn aside ‘by following other gods, which you have not known’ (verse 28).

He gives an instruction for later. “When the LORD your God brings you into the land you are entering to possess, you are to proclaim the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal” (verse 29). He says where the mountains are: across the Jordan, toward the sunset, near the Oak of Moreh (verse 30).

They are about to cross. When they have settled, they are to be careful to follow all that he is setting before them (verses 31-32).
passages.hearers:
Everything since chapter 6 has led here. Moses has preached love, memory and warning. Now he puts it as a plain choice between two ways.

In the Old Testament a blessing is more than good wishes. It is God's active favor, which brings life and fruitfulness. A curse is the opposite: that favor withdrawn. In the treaties of the ancient world the last part listed blessings for loyalty and curses for betrayal. Israel's covenant has the same ending.

Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal stand on either side of a valley in the central hill country, with the old town of Shechem between them. The place was not chosen at random. The Oak of Moreh, named in verse 30, was near Shechem, where God first appeared to Abraham in the land and promised it to him. Israel is to hold its ceremony at the spot where the promise was first given.

Setting the blessing on one mountain and the curse on the other made the choice something the people could see. The whole nation would stand in the valley with a mountain on each hand.

Chapter 27 gives the instructions for the ceremony, chapter 28 gives the blessings and curses in full, and chapter 30 puts the choice one last time. Here Moses only names it.

After this chapter the sermons pause, and the detailed laws begin.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua records that the ceremony was held: “Half of the people stood in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Ebal, as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded” (Joshua 8:33).

Genesis tells what had happened at that place long before: “Abram traveled through the land as far as the site of the Oak of Moreh at Shechem” (Genesis 12:6).

Mount Gerizim later became the holy mountain of the Samaritans. A Samaritan woman said to Jesus, “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain” (John 4:20), and he answered that a time was coming when people ‘will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem’ (John 4:21).

Paul sets this chapter's two words side by side when he writes of the cross: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), so that ‘the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles’ (Galatians 3:14).
passages.asks: Moses will not let the choice stay vague. Ask where you are trying to keep both ways open, a little of God and a little of something else. And think of the valley between the mountains. Ask what you would have to decide if you could see as clearly as Israel could where each road leads.
